sources.cite: AWS. Amazon EC2 User Guide: Instance recovery
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: 'If a system status check fails, AWS initiates automatic instance recovery'; it 'does not operate if only the instance status check fails'. Simplified automatic recovery is 'Enabled by default on supported instances' but 'Not supported for instances that attach instance store volumes at launch'; CloudWatch action based recovery 'Requires manual configuration', gives 'Faster recovery attempts' and 'Customizable notifications through SNS'. Preserved: instance ID, public, private and Elastic IP addresses, metadata, attached EBS volumes, Availability Zone. Lost: RAM and, for CloudWatch recovery, data on instance store volumes. The page gives no recovery times; the scenario's times are flagged teaching values.

sources.cite: AWS. CloudWatch User Guide: Create alarms to stop, terminate, reboot, or recover an EC2 instance
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: 'The recover action can be used only with StatusCheckFailed_System, not with StatusCheckFailed_Instance'; reboot is recommended for instance health check failures; 'avoid setting the same evaluation period for both a reboot alarm and a recover alarm. We recommend that you set recover alarms to two evaluation periods of one minute each and reboot alarms to three evaluation periods of one minute each'; 'Terminated instances cannot be recovered'.

brief.situation: Monday 09:00. lic-01 serves engineering software licenses for 300 designers, from one EC2 instance in us-east-2a (Ohio). It went down twice last month, both times at night, and each outage lasted hours until someone noticed. You are asked to make it heal itself.
handover: The vendor binds the license to the instance ID and private IP. A new instance needs a new license from the vendor, about a day's wait.
The license server keeps a cache it needs at start-up on the instance's local NVMe volume.
A heavy report job runs every night from 01:00 to 02:00. Target: 99.9% a month.
howItWorks: Learner-paced: nothing moves until you act. Investigate, set up recovery, then run the week.
The board shows the instance and its alarms; the meters show availability and downtime.
Before you run the week you are asked which failure gets which remedy. The debrief scores what you did.

FLAG: Outage while a recover alarm (2 one-minute periods) fires and the instance moves to new hardware. No AWS figure exists for this; it stands in for one and is a teaching value, not a measured one.

With an alarm notifying the on-call, a manual reboot about 30 minutes after the page.
With no alarm, the 03:10 hang is noticed when the designers start at 08:00.
Paged on-call stops and starts the instance on new hardware in about 45 minutes.
With no page, a host failure at 14:00 is reported by users and fixed in about an hour.
Rebuilding the license cache from backup after the instance store is lost takes about 2 hours.
A false reboot during the report job: 10 minutes down and the job rerun.
A replacement instance waits about a day for a new license from the vendor.
Availability over a 30-day month (2,592,000 s): 99.9% leaves 2,592 s (43.2 minutes).
One day per step of the week.

recQ.title: What survives recovery?
recQ.context: If lic-01 is recovered to new hardware, what does it keep?

choices.label: Its instance ID, IP addresses and EBS volumes; not memory or instance store data
choices.feedback: Right. Recovery keeps the identity the license is bound to, but RAM and, with alarm-based recovery, the instance store are lost; simplified recovery does not cover instance-store instances at all.

choices.label: Everything, including the local NVMe volume
choices.feedback: No. Instance store data does not move to new hardware; only EBS volumes and the instance's identity do.

plan.question: Before you run the week: which failure needs which remedy, and why does the instance store matter?

parts.label: Remedy per failure
parts.criteria: A host problem (StatusCheckFailed_System) is fixed by recovery to new hardware, keeping the instance ID and IP the license needs; an OS problem (StatusCheckFailed_Instance) by a reboot; recover alarm at 2 of 2 and reboot alarm at 3 of 3 one-minute periods to avoid a race; CPU is not a failure signal here; replacement breaks the license.
parts.modelAnswer: A failed system check means the host: recover it, which keeps the instance ID and IP. A failed instance check means the OS: reboot it. Set recover at 2 of 2 and reboot at 3 of 3 so they never race, and notify the on-call. CPU is high every night by design, and replacing the instance would void the license.

parts.label: The instance store
parts.criteria: Moves the license cache to EBS and to an EBS-only type, because instance store data is lost on recovery and simplified recovery does not cover instances with instance store at launch.
parts.modelAnswer: Recovery loses the instance store, and simplified recovery does not apply to an instance launched with one. Move the cache to EBS and change to m5.large in a short planned window; then both kinds of recovery work and keep the cache.

expertPath.text: History: one instance-check failure (OS), one system-check failure (host). Config: the cache is on the instance store. CPU: high nightly by design.
Recover alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System (2 of 2), reboot alarm on StatusCheckFailed_Instance (3 of 3), both to the on-call.
Move the cache to EBS and change to m5.large in a 15-minute window. The trade-off: 15 planned minutes now for recoveries that keep the cache later.

license.headline: The license was lost
license.body: Replacing a failed instance is right for stateless servers, but this license is bound to the instance ID. Recovery keeps the ID; replacement does not.

outage.headline: Long outages again
outage.body: Each failure needs its own remedy: recover for the system check, reboot for the instance check, and the cache off the instance store so recovery does not lose it.

fixed.headline: It heals itself
fixed.body: You read which checks failed, matched recover and reboot to them with non-racing periods, and moved the cache to EBS so recovery keeps it. That is the expert path.

partly.headline: Better, by a rougher route
partly.body: Check whether you read the history first, whether the cache is still on the instance store, and whether each check has its own action.

time_up.headline: No decision
time_up.body: The next failure waits for someone to notice.

scoring.modelReasoning: EC2 has two status checks. A failed system check is AWS's host: recover the instance to new hardware, which keeps its ID, IPs and EBS volumes, so a license bound to them survives. A failed instance check is the operating system: reboot it. CloudWatch allows the recover action only on StatusCheckFailed_System; AWS suggests recover at 2 of 2 and reboot at 3 of 3 one-minute periods so they never race. Instance store data is lost on recovery, and simplified automatic recovery does not cover instances launched with instance store, so move the cache to EBS. CPU is high every night by design and is no failure signal; replacing the instance would void the license.
